---
title: "Appendix J.2: Tree lifecycle submodule"
---

The main text follows trees through growth, senescence, death and decomposition. This appendix describes the lifecycle phases and the transitions between them.

TODO: update

::: {.table-block}

| Life cycle phase | Precolonial value | Introduced value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sprout | `<40 cm` trunk diameter at breast height (DBH) | `<40 cm DBH` | Standard classification for eucalyptus growth phases.[^1] |
| Mid-phase | `40-80 cm DBH` | `40-80 cm DBH` | Standard classification for eucalyptus growth phases.[^1] |
| Large | `>80 cm DBH` | `>80 cm DBH` | Standard classification for eucalyptus growth phases.[^1] |
| Large, old |  | We follow the same approach outlined by Croeser et al. (2025), who use allometric equations provided by the US Forestry Database (McPherson et al., 2016) and treat the maximum age of these equations as the point of "likely senescence". We use the allometric equation for *Ulmus americana* in the Pacific Northwest, USA, a related species of elm in a similar climate to Melbourne. | Croeser et al., 2025; McPherson et al., 2016 |
| Standing snag | Up to 50 years | Up to 50 years | Le Roux et al. (2014) conservatively estimate that dead trees could remain standing for at least 50 years after initial mortality, based on observations of the standing life of dead trees in *Eucalyptus* forests. |
| Fallen | `50-100 years` | `50-100 years` | Woldendorp and Keenan note that “CWD can persist for longer than these general estimates” and that decomposition depends on “wood durability, size”.[^2] `95%` decomposition for Australian eucalypt wood ranges from `7 years` for *E. regnans* to `375 years` for *E. camaldulensis* and *E. tereticornis*.[^2] Researchers note that decomposition can take several hundred years.[^3] Matthew J. Pringle et al. model a slow pathway and estimate `68 years` for `95%` of CWD to disappear.[^4] We therefore define whole fallen trees as lasting `50-100 years` and smaller decayed pieces as lasting `50-100 years`. |
| Decomposed | `50-100 years` | `50-100 years` | As above. |

:::

[^1]: Holland, 2024.
[^2]: Woldendorp, G., and Keenan, R. J. (2005). Coarse woody debris in Australian forest ecosystems: A review. *Austral Ecology*, 30(8), 834-843.
[^3]: Killey, P., Manning, A. D., Gibbons, P., Lindenmayer, D. B., and Fischer, J. (2010). Modelling fallen branch volumes in a temperate eucalypt woodland: implications for large senescent trees and benchmark loads of coarse woody debris. *Austral Ecology*, 35(8), 956-967.
[^4]: Pringle, M. J., Bray, S. G., and Carter, J. O. (2021). Modelling the disappearance of coarse woody debris, following a land clearing event. *Carbon Balance and Management*, 16, 36.
